name: Ninra Narayana Perumal Temple, Thiruthangal
deity: Vishnu as Ninra Narayana Perumal, standing, with the Goddess Senkamala Thayar
period: A Divya Desam of the Pandya country on the Thangal hill, sung by Bhoothathalvar and Thirumangai Alvar in the Nalayira Divya Prabandham
summary: On a low hill beside Sivakasi, Vishnu stands as Ninra Narayana Perumal, the lord who stayed — a Pandya-country Divya Desam sung by Bhoothathalvar and Thirumangai Alvar.

sections.history: Thiruthangal rises as a small rocky hill on the edge of Sivakasi in Virudhunagar district, and its crown carries the shrine of Ninra Narayana Perumal, one of the 108 Divya Desams of the Pandya Nadu. The temple was sung by Bhoothathalvar, one of the three earliest Alvars, and by Thirumangai Alvar, so its place in the Vaishnava tradition is very old. The Goddess, worshipped as Senkamala Thayar, the lady of the red lotus, is known by several names in local usage. The hill also holds a cave shrine, and in later centuries the temple was enlarged in the manner of the Pandya country, becoming the spiritual landmark of a town now better known for its industry.
sections.architecture: The temple is reached by steps up the Thangal hill, and its shrines are gathered on the rock above the town in the Dravidian style of the far south. In the sanctum the lord stands — the posture that gives him his name, Ninra Narayana, 'Narayana who stands' — with the Goddess in her own shrine. A cave shrine on the hill adds to the antiquity of the site.
sections.legends: The sthala purana links the name Ninra Narayana to the wedding of Usha and Aniruddha, grandson of Krishna: after Krishna overcame the asura Bana and freed Aniruddha, the couple begged the lord to remain, and he stayed here standing. Another tradition tells that the Goddess Sri came to this hill to do penance, and that the place is named Thiruthangal — 'where the sacred one stayed' — after her sojourn. Versions vary, but both speak of a lord who chose to remain.
sections.festivals: The temple keeps the Vaishnava festivals of the year, above all Vaikunta Ekadashi, with processions of the utsava deities around the hill and through the town. The days of Bhoothathalvar and Thirumangai Alvar, whose hymns sanctified the shrine, are honoured with recitation of their verses.
sections.experience: Climb the hill in the cool of early morning or at dusk, when the view over Sivakasi opens out below. The shrine is compact and intimate, and the standing lord is worshipped with quiet devotion. Thiruthangal combines well with Srivilliputhur, home of Andal and Periyalvar, a short drive to the west.

visit.timings: Open daily with morning and evening darshan sessions and a midday closure; Vaikunta Ekadashi is busiest. Confirm current timings before visiting.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional dress is expected — shoulders and knees covered; footwear removed before entering. Follow the posted rules and the priests' guidance.
visit.photography: Photography is restricted in and around the sanctum; follow the posted rules and the priests' guidance.
visit.gettingThere: Thiruthangal adjoins Sivakasi in Virudhunagar district, a few kilometres from the town centre. Sivakasi and Virudhunagar have railway stations, and Madurai Airport, about 75 km to the north-east, is the nearest airport.
